lecture_subjects: Price elasticity in consumers vs businesses
english_transcription:
Sales
SmartUp Foundations Course - Lecture 9
Given September 29th, 2024 by Yonatan Stern

Yonatan Stern: Okay, so we are at lecture number nine, which is pretty impressive — I think we got all the way here. And this time I would like to talk about sales. But before that, the usual introduction about our team: Ruti, Ayala, Livia, sitting there. And again, what is the program? I think everybody here knows it, so I can skip it. And as many of you know, when you give a lecture or presentation, you have to tell everybody what they're going to hear about. Then you tell them, and then you remind them. So that's what we're going to do. I'm going to tell you what we're going to talk about, then we'll talk about it, and then I'll give you the takeaways — the main things that I would really like you to remember. So we're going to talk about sales.

Yonatan Stern: And sales is a very complex subject because it has many situations and facets. So the first thing I wanted to do is divide it into two categories: direct sales and indirect sales, or sales channels. Direct sales also divides into two options. Option number one is e-commerce. Many of you know it — you want to buy something, you go on the web with your credit card and you buy it. And obviously there are salespeople. Usually, salespeople are called direct sales, but because I used the term already, I didn't call it that again. But if I say "direct sales" many times, I probably mean salespeople. Okay? And then there are sales channels. For example, when we sold CardScan, we had direct sales, but most of the sales were through retail. Then there are resellers, there are distributors, and there are partners.

Yonatan Stern: I will talk about each and every one of those, explain what they are, and explain the benefits and disadvantages of working with them. The next subject we're going to cover is demand generation, which is really critical. Nobody's going to buy your product unless you generate demand. That's a really important fact of life. If you don't generate demand, nobody's going to buy your product. And anybody who believes that somebody else is going to generate demand for their product is deluding themselves. And then there is the sales strategy. So I said there are options to do e-commerce or use salespeople — so which one? Do you want to go with e-commerce, or do you want to use salespeople? What are the strengths, weaknesses, benefits, and disadvantages of each one?

Yonatan Stern: We'll go into that and talk about it. Then there is the sales strategy and pricing, because at the end of the day there is a correlation between the packaging you do for the product, the pricing, and the ability to sell it — and they interact with one another all the time. We'll talk about that as well. And obviously, if we talk about pricing, then the question is price elasticity. You'd definitely want to sell a cup of coffee for $1,000, but probably most people will not buy it. If you sell it for $0.10, you're probably going to lose money. So there is a price elasticity, and we will discuss that. There's also price elasticity in business products. So there's the consumer side and there's the business side, and they don't behave the same way.

Yonatan Stern: What I'm going to show and demonstrate here is that price elasticity in consumers behaves very differently than the price elasticity — or lack thereof — of businesses. And when we talk about B2B, we all know B2B means business-to-business. But is the business, the consumer, the buyer, the same one? No. Because obviously, if you sell to a company, that's one thing. If you sell to a hospital, that's another thing. If you sell to a city, that's a third thing. And actually, there's almost an endless variety of potential buyers, and they all behave very differently. So when we say B2B, you have to understand who you're trying to sell to. And again, what are the benefits or disadvantages? Then there are the complexities of doing business-to-business sales. And I say it's two-dimensional.

Yonatan Stern: Why is it two-dimensional? Because when you sell to a company, the customer really is the company. But companies don't talk, companies don't move, companies don't make decisions — it's the people inside the company who do that. So first of all, you need to find the companies that are good prospects for your product because they can use it and it brings them value. And second, you need to figure out the people you need to talk to inside the company. So it's a much more complex sale than consumer, where it's the same person who is going to buy, use, and pay for the product. Then we're going to talk about things we've covered before, but this time I want to integrate them into the whole picture — which is the marketing funnel and the sales cycle.

Yonatan Stern: I've wondered many times why the sales cycle is called the "sales cycle" and not a "sales funnel." I have no idea — there's nothing cyclic about the sales. So I don't know why it's called a sales cycle, but that's the term everybody uses, so I use it too. Does anybody know why it's called the sales cycle?

Audience: Because when you close the deal, you need to start over with the next deal.

Yonatan Stern: So it's the salesperson's cycle, not the sales cycle. You're always selling something. Sometimes you're selling the meeting to get to the next proposal, to get to the deal, maybe. Okay.

Yonatan Stern: And while sales cycles are complex, we're going to talk about some of the elements of the sales cycle — not all of them — because it depends on different markets. Their sales cycles look different, the complexities of doing this. And then I'm going to bring a case study, which is IntelliChain, one of the companies working with us, and I want to show you how we changed their sales cycle to make it much more efficient than it used to be. I think it's going to be interesting, because after I tell you all the problems, it's good to look at some solutions. We'll talk about B2B pricing, then we're going to talk about the value of leads — what is the value of a lead and why is it so important? What do you do with leads, which we call lead processing? And obviously all of us want to sell in Israel, but we look at other countries — so how do we do international sales? And since sales cycles tend to be fairly long, we're going to talk about when you start the sales cycle and the cost of it. And if we still have time, we'll do major takeaways. As you can see, we have a very heavy agenda when we talk about sales — and you didn't even know that sales could be so complex.

Yonatan Stern: So I'll start with a question. What is the biggest asset of a company?

Audience: Salesperson.

Audience: Sales team.

Yonatan Stern: Okay, team. What else?

Audience: Brand.

Audience: Customers.

Yonatan Stern: Customers. What else?

Audience: Product.

Audience: Technology.

Audience: People.

Audience: Patents.

Yonatan Stern: The answer, to me, is customers and users. And I'm going to prove to you why customers and users are the biggest asset of a company. So let's talk about LinkedIn. LinkedIn was founded by Reid Hoffman. Reid Hoffman is one of the billionaires who came out of PayPal — the company that also produced Elon Musk, I believe. He started the company in 2003, and it was acquired in 2016. ZoomInfo started in 2000. We published our directory in 2004, and at that time we became somewhat of a competitor to LinkedIn. So I made the effort of going to California and meeting with Reid Hoffman, and what he told me was that he doesn't worry at all about being profitable — which, as you know, is like a physical blow to me, hearing that they don't worry about profitability. What he's worried about is the number of users he's going to have, and he's going to spend every penny he can get in order to increase that number. So they were acquired by Microsoft in 2016. At that time they had 433 million users, and they were acquired for $26 billion — which, if you divide one by the other, means Microsoft paid $60 per user.

Yonatan Stern: Let's take another example. WhatsApp started in 2009 and was sold in 2014 — five years. By the time they were sold, they had 55 employees. So employees can't account for that valuation. They were sold to Facebook, had 420 million users, most of them outside the US. WhatsApp was not well known in the US — it's still not as prevalent there as it is in Israel and other places. They were sold for $19 billion, which is $45 per user. When they were acquired, the founders had a very clear condition for the sale: there would be no advertising. There was a huge fight over it. There's still no advertising on WhatsApp because of that. So Facebook struggled for many years figuring out how to make money from it. We'll talk later about what I think they do today to make money. In the beginning, they were just focused on increasing the number of users — that's it. And five years later, they took the money and were happy.

Yonatan Stern: Waze started in 2008 and was acquired by Google five years later, in 2013. Fifty million users, $1.1 billion sale. I'm not aware of any revenue stream for Waze, and Google paid $22 per user.

Yonatan Stern: So I hope I've convinced you that users and customers are what's important. But the question is why. Why these crazy valuations?

Audience: These prices are just because of the users, not because of the technology?

Audience: They paid different prices per user.

Yonatan Stern: Yeah, but it is because of the users. And I'll answer this. It is very hard to get customers and users. All of us in business know that it is really hard to get customers and users, and people are willing to pay a lot of money for them. Bear in mind that getting 400 million users is a phenomenal accomplishment. So I talk about customers and users — and what is the difference? Users are the people using the product. Like Google Search — you go to Google, you don't pay any money, you use it. Facebook, WhatsApp, Waze, LinkedIn, Instagram — all of these have users who don't pay money. They're not really the customers. They are the users of these products. And the customers are those who pay money — for advertisements, besides WhatsApp. It depends — it's not that simple.

Yonatan Stern: So advertising — clearly. Google has AdWords, Meta Ads, and all of that. LinkedIn has ads as well. That's the obvious one that people do. But there are many other business models that take users and convert them into customers. So let's talk about a few of them, and I'll talk about this path even more later on. They start with users that either pay no money or pay very little — they are the users. But when a company sees that there are many users inside a company, they turn it into a business sale by differentiating the two products. Zoom is doing it — you can have a free product that everybody uses, but there's also an upgrade. LinkedIn Sales Navigator is another example, in addition to their ads. WhatsApp for Business is the new thing with WhatsApp. I don't know if you've noticed, but many businesses are now using WhatsApp as a kind of chatbox and also for distributing information. So they start making money without ads. Slack, obviously. And there are others. I keep listing Waze because I have no clue how they make money — if it's advertisements only, I've never received one. I barely use it, so I honestly don't know.
Now, if you have noticed, there are many businesses that start using WhatsApp as kind of a checkbox and also for distributing information. So they start making money without ads. Slack, obviously. And there are others. I keep putting Waze because I have no clue how they make money. So if anybody knows, I've never received an advertisement because I never touch it. I just don't know.

So if anybody knows, I don't know. My idea is that they should sell it — obviously, to any city planner that wants to know how many people go from this street to this place, if you want to build bus routes, and so forth. Anyway, so what's the path to having customers? We talked about the value of customers, so what's the path to doing that? I've separated between customers and users, but in most situations that we are familiar with, they are the same, or at least they work for the same company. If you remember when I talked about the complexities of B2B sales, I said the customer — the money — is the company. But then there are the people who need to make the decision. So they work for the company, but they are not the same as the user.

And then there's the demand generation process. I will talk about it a lot more during the presentation. Demand generation is always, always the responsibility of the company that created the product. Okay? That is really important for anybody that starts a company. If you believe somebody else is going to do your job, you live in a different world. Even though people tell you that they're going to do this, it's not true. Companies need to create their own channels and never rely on someone else to create demand. You put your product in a store — I will talk about that later and give you examples — because I happened to make the stupid mistake of selling CardScan through retail, and I learned a lot of things doing that. We did a lot of programs in the stores to convince salespeople to promote our product, recommend our product — nothing.

You have to create your own demand. And we come back to something you will hear many times: you have to start with branding, because if nobody has heard about you, then nobody's going to buy your product. We'll talk about that as well.

So let's talk about sales channels. As I said, on the direct side — when a company itself sells the product — there are two options, at least. One is e-commerce on the company website, and the other is salespeople. And salespeople also have two options. Option number one is outreach: you start making phone calls. Many companies have what's called a BDR or SDR — Business Development Rep or Sales Development Rep. And that poor person is hitting the phones hoping that somebody will answer. That's outreach. Inbound is different. The company is doing demand generation programs, and people who are interested in the product raise their hand, fill out a form, say "please call me" or something like that. And then the salesperson calls them back or interacts with them. So those are the two options for direct sales.

For indirect sales, as I said, there are several. Let's start with retailers. I'll tell you a little bit about what we did at CardScan because I think it's really interesting. When we started with CardScan, I had kind of a product — it wasn't really working well, but it was there. And one day, I remember it was a Friday, there was a knock at the door and a nice young lady walked in and said, "I'm working for American Airlines magazine." Turns out there is an American Airlines magazine — the one they put in the seat pocket in front of you. What, there is a whole company for that? Yes, American Airlines magazine. They have a new magazine every two weeks. And she had remnant space. You'll learn a little bit about marketing from this presentation. Remnant space is when it's about time to close the magazine and print it, and they have empty space for ads. So if you open the newspaper and you see on the back page an ad for [unclear], you know that they failed to sell that space. Instead of leaving it empty, they put all kinds of filler ads about themselves or something like that. Basically, they just don't leave a space empty. That's called remnant space.

She said, "I can give you a half page for" — I don't remember — a low price, "but you have to give me the graphics and the ad itself in three or four days." I didn't have anything. We did it anyway. We put the ad in, and we included what's called an offer code. So if you called us on the phone — because we weren't in any store or anything — if you called us and gave the offer code, we'd give you a discount, whatever it was. And to my utter surprise, two weeks went by and the phone never rang. It was three people in the company: me, the developer, and another person. Whenever the phone rang, we all jumped at it, and it was usually something unimportant. The phone just never rang.

Week three, the phone doesn't ring. Week four, the phone started to ring. And to this day we don't understand why the airline magazines always worked with a three-week delay. Don't ask me why. We advertised in the airline magazines for years, and it was always a three-week delay. I don't know why, but it started working and we started expanding. At the time I'm talking about, we were spending $100,000 a month putting ads in all the airline magazines and in other magazines. That's expensive. But we already had a few hundred stores in the US carrying our product and committed to selling it. And my CFO, Mark Girolamo, around February or March every year, would say, "Jonathan, why do we spend so much money? It's ridiculous. Why don't we go from full-page ads to half-page ads and save half the money?" We'd argue for a few weeks and he would win. We'd cut the ads. Nothing happened. He'd say, "See? Sales are the same, no problem whatsoever." March — same. April — same. May — started declining. June declines a lot more. July — he gets nervous and says, "Maybe we go back to full-page ads." So we go back to full-page ads, and sales start to grow. Come February or March the following year, same thing. On the third year, I said, "Mark, you're an idiot. We've done this twice already. Enough is enough." The point is: you have to generate demand. There's nothing you can do about it. You have to generate demand.

Later on, I was already running ZoomInfo. I brought in a very talented guy — you will hear his name later on — Peter Wayman, to run CardScan. He said, "I don't know anything about retail. I don't understand it, so I'm going to bring in a really smart guy." And he brought in the VP of marketing from Bose, the speaker company. The guy was really good. He understood exactly how you do direct sales. He started advertising remnant space on television, on the radio, all of that. And sales started to take off, which I think is proof that no matter how good your product is — and to give you the opposite example: I said, who is going to use CardScan? People who work in the office, like lawyers, like this. So we hired a salesman and gave him the job of going into downtown Boston, building to building, knocking on doors, and trying to sell CardScan for a whole month. He went door to door, demoed the product, and sold a grand total of zero. Not a single unit. So if you ask why getting customers is so important, it takes a tremendous amount of effort, and it's not that simple.

So — retailers. Don't think that getting into the store means it's going to sell anything.

Resellers. A lot of people think that if you're based in Israel and want to sell internationally, you need to find resellers in those countries. You're smiling — I guess you've been there, right? Yes, but no. Let me tell you another story.

When we were at ZoomInfo, there was a company called Monster. Monster had a large database of resumes. Job seekers would put their resume in Monster, and virtually every HR department in America used it to find candidates — what LinkedIn is today. But you had to upload your resume and specify what you wanted. What Monster didn't have was people who were not looking for a job, and executive recruiters wanted to find exactly those people. These are called passive candidates, and passive candidates are obviously what people want — because if you're not looking for a job, you must be good. If you're looking for a job, you must be... eh, right?

So we went to Monster. We talked to them many times and made a deal. We became partners and resellers — they would sell our product, telling customers, "We have this active job seeker product and this passive job seeker product, and you can buy the whole package together and cover the entire market." Great deal. The reseller cut was 30 to 40% of our price. We were very excited about it, and we sold a total of — you already know where this is going — zero. And that really bothered me. They had maybe 100 salespeople sitting in a room. So we decided to do something about it. I took one of our best people and placed her inside Monster. I said, "Work with their salespeople, listen to what they say, and help them sell." She sat there for two weeks and changed the results from zero to zero.

So I asked what was going on. And she gave me the insight you should take with you. She said, "Listen — if I go to a customer and say I have this $10,000 product for active job seekers, and the customer buys it, Monster gets $3,000 because we take 30%. You take $7,000. I get 10% commission — so I sold a $10,000 deal and I get $300. It's just not interesting." You have to generate your own demand.

Distributors are very similar to resellers and partners. So that's another sad story. That was resellers — now I'll talk about partners. By the way, if it wasn't so cold in here, I'd take my coat off and you'd see all the scars on my back. Everything I'm telling you here is firsthand lessons.

So we had CardScan, and CardScan was very good software. One day we got a phone call from a company called Visioneer. They had invented a phenomenally fast scanner with software — that's why it's called PaperPort. And because of their scanner, you could scan business cards as well. They wanted to include our software with it. After a lot of negotiations, they agreed to pay a dollar per copy of our software. Here's the product — a nice scanner. And here's the software. Those of you who can't read from back there, I'll make it bigger: you can see CardScan. CardScan. CardScan. They paid us a dollar per copy included in the box, and we were very excited about it. A few months later I get a call from them: "We don't really believe that including CardScan is increasing PaperPort sales, so we can't pay you a dollar anymore — we'll pay you fifty cents." Fifty cents is better than nothing, so fine. A few months later, same phone call: "We really can't pay you anything. If you still want to put it in the box — and it does cost us money for the printing and everything — okay, do it for zero." Fine, we'll do that.
...didn't really believe that increasing the sales of Visioneer PaperPort — we won't be able to pay you a dollar. We'll pay you half a dollar. Half a dollar is better than nothing. So fine, okay.

A few months later, another phone call, saying: "Really, we can't pay you anything. If you still want to put it in here, it costs us money." Remember the book and everything? Okay, for zero — fine, we'll do that.

A few more months later, I get the famous phone call and he says, "Listen, what you should do is create a light version that you put in our box, and then an upgrade that you'll make money from — because we're going to charge you a dollar for every unit that you put in there." By the way, they went bankrupt. So that was my little revenge on them.

If you didn't get the point that you have to create demand for your own product, I think I just proved it with all the scars on my back. So it is critical for a company to own its customers.

And we had this situation with Intellij — I'll talk about them later — where many resellers came to them and wanted to resell their product. And I told them, "That's fine, except for one little thing that you should ask. You should say: 'That's fine, except that the customer is ours, so they sign on our contract, not on your contract.'" And lo and behold, all of these resellers just disappeared, because what they really wanted was the customer — the product of Intellij was just the hook to get to the customer. The customers should have a relationship with your company. This is really critical.

Many companies treat customer service as a liability. I think that's a huge mistake. Very rarely do customers call you — honestly, that's fairly rare. Even if your product stinks, they just don't call. So when somebody calls, you better make sure they are delighted after that phone call, because it's worth a lot of money.

So people who move their customer support to India, or wherever — in my mind, make a big mistake. The company should focus on a strong brand. I say that every single meeting: demand generation is the growth engine. If there is a single most important growth engine, it's your demand generation programs and delighted customers.

So I said there are two ways of doing direct business: e-commerce and salespeople. How do you decide which one to take? Actually, it's not that complicated, because there are certain things that would make you take one direction and other things that take you the other direction — and it's really hard to even mix them.

First of all, it depends on the type of customer and the price of the product. If you sell a consumer product — B2C — there's a good chance you'll probably go with e-commerce. If you sell B2B, we'll cover that in a moment. But it can also be both, and both are, in my mind, really interesting.

If you're B2C, then usually you sell at a low price. Consumers usually don't pay thousands of dollars for anything. If they do pay thousands of dollars for something, usually it comes with payment terms that spread it out. I mean, if you buy a car, a lot of people lease a car. Why do they lease a car? Because they can handle paying 2,000–3,000 shekels a month — they cannot handle paying 160,000 shekels. So usually consumers pay very low prices online.

A few hundred shekels, maybe 1,000 shekels. And nobody is calling consumers to buy a product. You would very rarely have the phone ring and somebody trying to sell you, I don't know, a dishwasher. It just doesn't happen. So it's very clear how these things behave.

B2B is usually at much higher prices — a few thousand dollars. And I'll explain in a moment why they have to be at a much higher price.

So let's look at e-commerce. What's good and bad about it? First and foremost, the product should be self-explanatory, because there's nobody to answer questions. So if you have a very sophisticated new algorithm — some B2B thing — nobody's going to buy it online because they don't understand what you're doing. It doesn't work. So it has to be easy to understand, and low price. I put it at about $1,000, but it's usually much lower than that.

It's totally dependent on a strong brand, because the customer has to go on their own initiative to your website. If they've never heard about you, they won't come — they won't stumble upon it. And so it really depends on demand generation activities: whether you put ads in airline magazines — which is what we did, by the way. It worked only in airline magazines. All the other magazines just didn't do anything. Don't ask me why, but we tried a million magazines. Nothing worked. Just airline magazines.

It works 24/7, so unlike salespeople, it doesn't go home. You can continue to sell. It's very efficient. The only cost you have is the credit card commission, and it's a fixed price. You will see that in B2B, negotiation is the heart of the matter. When it's e-commerce, there's nobody to negotiate with — you either pay that price or you don't, and you buy it. So that's why e-commerce is good. But remember, I'm applying this really to very specific items you can sell through there.

Salespeople are almost a must when you have a new product, a new idea, something more complex. There's just no way of selling it without human interaction, without somebody explaining what the product does. So if you are in a SaaS business or you develop a new technology, a new engine, whatever it is, you'll probably have to demonstrate it and answer questions.

The price might be high — and here's the reason: salespeople want to make money. For some bizarre reasons, they do want to make money. Bizarre, bizarre. I don't know — I like to work with salespeople... they just do it for the love of it. But I couldn't find those. So I just took $100,000, which is kind of the low end for salespeople. So to make $100,000 a year — and you want to make money too — each salesperson needs to sell $500,000. That means 20% of every dollar you sell goes to the salesperson.

I think the average is actually twice both amounts. Yeah, usually. But you're right — $200,000 for a salesperson is high. You can get them, and I'll come back later and show how you can get people for $100,000. There is a way. But think about it: if they need to sell $500,000 a year, that's about $50,000 a month, and if each deal is $5,000, that means they have to do ten deals a month — two deals a week. That's really difficult.

So what happens is that, usually, if you want to use salespeople, the price of the product is much higher than $5,000 — as you said, $10,000, $20,000, and so forth. At ZoomInfo, we sold at a $2,000 minimum price, or $1,800 actually. And I'll explain in a moment how we did that. But that's generally why B2B sales are much more expensive — because you have to use a salesperson, and the salesperson wants to make money. The rest is history. So the economics only work for a large deal.

But there is a benefit to using salespeople, which is that it's much easier to start. You take a salesperson, throw them into the water, and they start working. Why? Because just by making a lot of phone calls, they can get somewhere. The easiest demand generation is to just become a pest and keep calling people and talking to them. So it can work for all companies. When I started — and it was B2B — I started with salespeople. Usually it worked, but it's far from ideal, and you'll see in a moment why. It's also easier to reach profitability because the deal sizes are much higher.

Okay. So that's the benefit of going with e-commerce, what you have to give up, and what's going on with salespeople. But in some cases you can do both, and those are, in my mind, the most interesting ones.

So it's very hard to combine e-commerce with salespeople. I'll explain why it's hard, and later I'll show how it's done. Usually — as I said, ZoomInfo. So let's start with another story. This time it's five scars on my back, because I tried it five times and failed miserably five times.

So we started with salespeople. When I built the company back in 2000, by 2001 we had a salesperson. By 2002, we had $1 million in sales from that salesperson, and then we became profitable. So it worked really well. Then we added more and more salespeople. Remember — salespeople need to sell $500,000, they need to make money, all the good things.

And then we said, "We need to start selling online." I mean, CardScan is not complicated — it's just names of people with phone numbers. Give me a break. You don't have to be a rocket scientist to understand what it does. And we also had a lot of leads because we published a directory of all the people. Anybody who searched for, say, Jonathan Stern on the web, in most cases the first result was ZoomInfo — and it says, "Here's the phone number. Click here." When you click, it says, "Buy it." Really straightforward, nothing sophisticated.

So we were dying to make a product you could buy online. But how do you differentiate between what the salespeople are selling and this product? I mean, it's basically just getting data. So the obvious answer was: let's differentiate. If you buy online, you can get 50 records a month. If you buy from a salesperson, you get 1,000, 2,000, whatever — I don't remember the exact numbers. So that's what we did — we differentiated on quantity.

And about two days after we released the product, the salespeople were demonstrating in front of my office with big signs, sitting on strike, and explaining to me that this was ridiculous. One of them said, "I have a quota — you want me to sell $50,000 a month. I almost closed a $10,000 deal. I called the customer to sign the deal, and he says, 'You know, I just discovered on your website that I can try this product for $99.'" I said, "Yeah, but it's not the same product — you only get 50 records." And the customer said, "It's okay, I'll start with that, see if I like it, see if I need more, and then I'll get back to you." He says, "I lost five customers just this morning. If you want me to continue selling at this company, you take that stupid thing off."

So that's what I did. I tried again a year later. Hilat tried it a gazillion times. We did it together. Never succeeded — never. Because the product was not differentiated enough. Quantity was not enough, and the price mismatch — $10,000 or $5,000 versus $99 — people just said, "Forget it, I'll just try it online, it costs less." I don't remember all the logic, but we gave up in the end. I dropped it.

And that actually allowed a lot of our competitors to go into the market. So Apollo and Lusha and all of these companies used that weakness and went to market using it. But I'm just telling you a bit of the story.

So what are the successful ones? The successful ones do it the opposite way. What they do is start with online products that you can buy and use, and then the salespeople step in. To understand, you need to feel it. We just had a conversation with Yarden about an idea. And I said, Yarden, you have to be in every phone call, in every meeting. So let's talk about the case study, because I try to give you as many examples as possible, because they show you more than anything else. So we have a company that joined Smartup. Elan is here. There is a market for it. There are known players. Usually the product is sold at around a low few hundred thousand dollars — 100, 200, $250,000 — from the existing players. And they are very sophisticated, high-end products. And basically they play in the S&OP market. I asked several times, what is S&OP? It sounds sophisticated. It's basically Sales and Operations Planning. So not that sophisticated, but it sounds really good. And what is their claim to fame?

When they joined us about a year and a half ago, they told us, well, the big guys go after the big companies, but the low end of the market is underserved. So if we go to the smaller companies — smaller in their terminology was a company like $25 million to $50 million, $100 million — and if we give it at a low price, we're going to break the market. Okay, so the high end, as I said, is $100,000 and up. They wanted to sell for $10,000. They also developed a very nice, sleek, modern-looking user interface, great algorithms inside to do the prediction and the forecasting, more accurate based on the past. So they take the history of the last year and based on that history, they try to predict what's going to happen this year.

They mix it with information about campaigns that the company is going to do, events that are going to happen and so forth, and create this. And it's also easy to integrate because they go through files — Excel files — which mitigates the issues of IT departments that don't want to integrate into their systems. And it's also making it very simple. So it basically should sell like hotcakes. Right, Elan? Hot cakes. Absolutely. So let's see what happens. The founder, Oe, who is not here today — he's at a conference — he knows the business. He was a consultant at Ernst & Young in their S&OP practice. And he's also a lecturer at Azrieli College of Engineering in Jerusalem. Right? Yeah. Okay, so he likes teaching. He really likes teaching. He has delivered many courses, enjoys it. And when they came to me, they also had two design partners.

But these design partners refused to buy. They kept giving all kinds of reasons why the product is not perfect yet. And they had a lot of sales cycles, but they didn't converge to anything. The sales cycle — remember, the sales cycle process included a proof of concept. So they would give the product to the customer for a month, support the customer through that month, in order to prove that it really works. So after all of that hard work, we sat down to analyze why it was not working. Really. Even the design partners didn't buy, and things just took forever. And the first conclusion we came to was: we think this is a really hot market, but the reality is most of our customers live in the Middle Ages — they had no clue what we were really talking about.

So they used spreadsheets and basically said, okay, last October we sold this amount. This year we'll do 5% more. So let's multiply every line by 5%, and here's the prediction and the forecast for this year. Literally, that's what happened in many companies. Was it accurate? No. But how can you predict the future? It's the future, right? At the same time, customers are not idiots. So they wanted to understand what the right process really is. They were hungry for education and knowledge. And what we did with the new approach was to leverage the capabilities of the founders to address the problems of the market. There was a reason I told you that Oe likes to teach — because he's a really good teacher.

People love him as a teacher. He had courses that he had already given, and lectures he had already given. So we started selling these courses. And that, basically, instead of cold calling — where the customer on the other side has no patience because it's a sales call and they're not going to listen — if they paid 2,000 shekels to attend, they listen. So what we did is we took the cold calling and instead asked people to pay us money, come to a meeting — a Zoom or a physical one. We sell both. We actually sell a lot of on-site courses to companies. So the company buys in, they have 20 or 30 people in the room, and we teach them what S&OP and demand planning is and so forth.

And the other thing we realized was that the competitors in the market had a broken process for the stage of the market. What is a broken process? They have a reseller who knows the product, but doesn't really understand S&OP. He knows how to install it and how it works, but beyond that, he doesn't know anything. They don't give any support to the process — they give support for installing it. It works, you know, I turned it on, it does work. I'm fine, I'm done. But the customer didn't know what to do with it. So we started creating these three legs: knowledge, methodology, and technology. So we train you, we teach you, we support you, we are with you, we actually help you do the work, and we give you technology. And that was unique. No competitors in Israel do that.

So that was interesting. We now make about $20,000 to $30,000 a month just from selling the courses. We took the POC that was free, we repackaged it, and instead we call it a Value Analysis Program. We charge $7,200 — even though I requested they make it as close to $10,000 as possible, but they refused. But we do sell those. And now the sales cycle, instead of us paying for the entire process, we basically turned every step of the sales cycle into a product that people pay for. And people listen more because they pay. So this is just an example. It's not huge genius or whatever. It's just: be honest, look at the situation, and say, the market is embryonic. We're selling to people who just don't really understand what we're trying to do.

I can keep preaching, but it doesn't help. So how about we turn the weakness into a strength — suddenly educate the market, but have them pay for it, so they appreciate the knowledge they get and appreciate what they receive. And it seems to be working really well. We also raised the price, because $10,000 sounds like rickety nothing. If the others want $100,000 or $200,000, we cannot go with $10,000 because it cheapens what we do. So we now have the product sold at $50,000. Just to give you an example of how you take a problem, look it in the eye, be the CEO trying to sell the product, and be honest with yourself — or objective enough — to really understand why it is not working. And it wasn't working. We will probably do about $400,000 in 2024.

Not bad for a company that joined us about a year and a half ago. Okay. B2B pricing. Going back to my previous example of how I negotiated with that poor salesman — within reason, companies are less sensitive to price than people assume. Why? Because unless it's a commodity product where you understand the pricing, it's always something you have no way of really understanding what you're paying for. So you just make a gut decision. Second — and this is really what they're sensitive to — customers are not so much sensitive to the price itself. They don't always tell you that. But what was the IBM saying? FUD — Fear, Uncertainty, and Doubt. IBM didn't invent it, but they perfected it.

So when they sat with a customer — talking now about a mainframe in the sixties or seventies — the whole bank is going to depend on this machine. The CIO who bought the machine took a big risk, because if that mainframe fails, the bank stops. One glitch and the bank loses days of business. High risk. IBM took advantage of that, and they would say, well, you need to buy a mainframe, right? Your bank needs a mainframe. Nobody is ever going to blame you if an IBM machine failed, because you bought the best. There's nothing better than an IBM mainframe. Fear, uncertainty, doubt. Machines fail. You don't want to be there explaining to the CEO why you bought a Burroughs or a CDC or a Prime computer. You want to say, I bought the best there is.

That's what bothers the people who make the decision — the risk they're taking. Performance: will it really solve the problem? I understand everything you're saying, but will it really solve my problem? Don't show me demos, don't tell me all these stories. Will it really solve my problem? And they can't answer that unless they buy it. But that's what really bothers them. And the third one — which people don't talk about — the total cost of ownership is far bigger than what we think, because they need to change the behavior of the people who use it. They used spreadsheets. Now we want them to use software. Will they be able to use software? Will I have to fire them? If I fire them, they've worked for us for 20 years — people will get angry. There are all kinds of ramifications to a product you're going to put in the company that they don't share with you and will never share with you.

The price is usually the last issue. They use the price because it's easy to talk about, right? And anyway, why not get the discount? But in reality, it's not their personal money. We're talking about a company. They're not taking the money out of their own pocket, and they will always negotiate the price. So when you do a B2B deal, these are the issues: performance, risk, and total cost of ownership — not in terms of money, but in the total chaos it can bring to the organization. And payback is always hard to show. So I have a solution. It doesn't always work, but I'll tell you a story about it.

What do I mean by "trivialize it"? When I was in the US, there was an advertisement on TV. In the ad was a little kid — he was crying and he looked horrible. And they just said, for the price of one cup of coffee a day, you can save this kid. They trivialized it. One little cup of coffee and this child will be saved. Wouldn't you do that? Now think about it — a cup of coffee at Starbucks is $5, times 365. You're close to $2,000. If I told them it's going to cost you $2,000 a year to save him, they'd say, screw it — he's a nice guy, right?

If I told them it's going to cost you $2,000 a year to save him, they'd say, screw it, he's a nice guy, right?

Yeah, but when you have 100 salespeople, it starts to be $8,000. It's $100,000 a year. It's a lot of money — because they ask for all the money for the year on day one. But you trivialize it. So that's the way to handle the shock of the price. And also, as I said before, when you come in with a low price, when the market is well-known, it always sends a double message. It's cheap, but why is it cheap? And the "why is it cheap?" is not always in your favor. So what do we want to do — use leads or cold calling? It depends. You want to do cold calling?

Okay, you stay here afterwards, I want you here. But most people prefer leads, obviously. Why? Because you get the contact information. They tell you, here's my phone number or my email, call me — they give you permission to talk to them, and they have intent. Obviously, leads are far better than cold calling. And I go back to what I said many times about growth engines. Lead generation is the most important growth engine you're ever going to have in your company. If there's anything you want to think about day and night, before you go to bed, inside the bed when you dream — it's lead generation. Lead generation will make or break your company, and it's the most efficient way to initiate a sales process. The guy says, talk to me. What can be better than that?

But there's an impact beyond that which I really want to talk about, because Peter Weyman, the guy I keep mentioning — he's a genius — taught me that it simplifies the process of hiring salespeople. Why do salespeople command high salaries? Because they come and they tell you, I have ten years of experience. I know how to prospect. I know how to get to customers. I know how to convince them. I know how to close the sales cycle. I deserve every penny you give me. In reality, they don't. But if you want to hire B players — that's the B right there — what you need to do is basically make them deal closers instead of deal initiators. They hate to do cold calling. Virtually all the salespeople who swore to me that their biggest delight in life is cold calling were lying. They hate it.

They don't do it. They tell you they do it, but they don't — because it's an ugly job to do cold calling. And if they start with cold calling, they need to get the prospect interested. It's very difficult to sell a product to somebody who has no patience for you. You cold called. You got him in the middle of something. He has no patience. It's very different when he says, talk to me, right? So when he says talk to me, you're already in the middle of your sales cycle. He wanted you to talk. If you're just a human being who speaks English, nice degree — you graduated college — you are just a fine salesman for me, and I can replace you anytime I want, because you don't bring tremendous value. You just know your job.

That's all you do. And that's what happened at ZoomInfo when we started growing like crazy and we had leads coming in — 20,000 leads a month. Peter Weyman hired them in groups of ten, put them in a class, and got them to full quota within three months. From not knowing anything about ZoomInfo to hitting full quota — they had three months to figure it out. Why? Because they got their leads. We told them what to do. If you don't get to full quota, you're not a B minus, you're a C maybe. And it worked. It just worked. So as a growth engine, if you have good leads coming in, you have a growth engine that you can leverage.

I go back to the beginning and talk about what happens if you turn your lead generation into lead generation on steroids — which means you have free or low-cost products as the lead, so the customer is already using your product. Then the salespeople really have very little to do. They just call and say, I see you have four people using Zoom. We have all of these great features for business. It's very easy to do. Zoom has a real consumer product — it's free for consumers — and they have a brilliant differentiator. The differentiator that I love is the 40 minutes. After 40 minutes, the call is disconnected. For most users, it doesn't matter — mom, I'll call you back. Nothing happened. But if you are on a very important call with a prospect and suddenly it cuts off, you look like an idiot.

You will never allow yourself to look like that when you talk to a prospect or any potential investor. So I think it's brilliant. LinkedIn did a great job too. They got all the people to say, that's my official résumé, my official professional presence. And then they built Sales Navigator on top of it. They have a product for recruiters and obviously advertising on top of that. Slack again — they had a brilliant idea. You can use Slack as much as you want, as many people as you want. It's really great. Except that we only keep history for the last two weeks. Most companies use Slack as their corporate memory. Remember three months ago I already asked you to fix that bug? See here, look. And you said yes, and you didn't. Okay, two weeks just doesn't serve that purpose. But it works for as many users as you want, and everything is great — and everybody upgrades because of a feature that makes it not quite right for business use, but not too irritating for regular use. Okay, HubSpot — I use the free product. It's not great, honestly. But they do have one.

Leads. Okay — leads must be called back within five minutes. And I mean five minutes. Why? Because as much as I praised the lead, the person isn't necessarily that interested. He saw something on the web, he clicked, and he remembers it for about five minutes. If you call him an hour later, he says, what? Intellichain? Are you sure? I'm not sure what you're talking about. They don't remember, because it wasn't high on their priority list — let's face it. So if you don't call within five minutes, your chances of reaching that person and having a conversation go down by 80%. We checked it. Second — in those same five minutes, he's still where he was before. So he'll answer because he's still looking at the web.

So what we did at ZoomInfo — the leads would come in, and I'll show you what we did. The first thing we did was lead enhancement, lead enrichment. A lead comes in — it says Jonathan Sterna, ZoomInfo email address. That's it. Interesting? Not interesting? I don't know. But what we did is we added two dimensions of data — on the person and on the company. On the person, you add two things. Number one is anything you can find about the person, usually in terms of title. As I said before, if the title was Director or VP of Sales, they got a callback from a salesperson, not from a BDR. But there's also a lot of information about history. Remember, I talked about six touch points. Those touch points are usually captured by the marketing automation system. And you want to add all of that information — this person has been on your website five times, six times, ten times — that's better than someone you've never seen before. And about the company, as I said, you collect a lot of data and you want to add it to this.

And what you do with all of that is you give it a score. You calculate a score for the lead, and based on the score, you do distribution. The distribution we did at ZoomInfo was the following: if the score was low, it went to a BDR. Actually, the BDRs were the same people who did customer support and customer service — so we gave them something more interesting to do than just deal with problems. They also got some commission out of it, and they knew the product very well, obviously. And we did close a good amount of business from that — but it was small deals, $1,000, $2,000, $3,000 deals, because we knew in advance it was a low-end lead. The higher-end leads we sent to the salespeople. They had to call back within five minutes. If they didn't call back within five minutes, the lead automatically routed to the next salesperson, and that salesperson was penalized. We knew who was on the phone — our system knew who was on the phone — so we didn't send it to people who were already on a call. We only sent it to people who indicated they were available. So I'm just giving you a sense of how a sales process is built as it grows.

International sales. Israel is great — it has about 10 million people — but it's not as large an economy as we would like it to be. So my advice to companies is: the second market you want to go after is the US. Why not the first? Why Israel first? Because they speak Hebrew and they sit right here, and they're usually more honest about why your product isn't good. They will tell you it sucks even if your product is great. So if you really want a harsh experience, sell in Israel — they will tell you you're an idiot and you don't know what you're doing. And if they buy from you, you're going to be very successful in America. It's just easier. Remember I talked about starting with sales when you have no product — you're at the very embryonic stage when you start talking to your friends here and calling people and so forth. I want people to start selling on day one. They have no product. They have no clue what they're doing. They have to start selling. The CEO who doesn't sell shouldn't call himself a CEO.

So why the US? Very large, uniform market. Uniform — meaning they all speak English. It's the same laws, same rules, same stuff. Even though there are 50 states, in most cases they are very similar. It's the largest market in the world — that is a unique market. The European market is large, but it's divided into many countries. Americans speak English — and we've just proven that many people in this room understand English. They're sophisticated, in most cases tech-savvy, and they're very polite, so that's good. And they are familiar to us — there are a lot of people here who feel comfortable in American culture.

Branding is international by nature. When you start doing branding activities, you don't even think about it, but they're international by definition. You put something on LinkedIn, it goes anywhere — to anyone who sees it. Google, LinkedIn, Facebook are all international platforms. Unless they're blocking Israeli content, it will arrive wherever it needs to arrive. Also, most connections and meetings today are done electronically. Salespeople used to have a territory — territory as in land. Why territory? Because they would hop in the car and drive to see customers. Location was very important. We sold $100,000 deals at ZoomInfo and never saw the customer. Never. And we're not unique. Most companies today never see the customer face to face. They see them through Zoom, but they don't physically meet the customer. Okay.
Salespeople used to have a territory. Territory is land. Why territory? Because they would hop in the car and drive to see the customers. So location was very important. We sold at Zoom — $100,000 deals — never saw the customer. Never. And we were not unique. Most companies today never see the customer face to face. They see them through Zoom, but they don't see the customer in person.

Most presentations and demonstrations are anyway done via Zoom, so there's no benefit to me showing up, opening my suitcase, taking out a computer and showing them on the screen. I can do that by Zoom anyway, right? And the need for a personal one-on-one meeting is really minimal. Why? Because from the customer's side, if you come to a meeting, the other side knows they're going to spend an hour with you — because you traveled, you came, and it's to greet you, give you coffee, chitchat. An hour went by. When you're on Zoom, they tell you, "I have 15 minutes," and it's polite. Nobody is going to be insulted if you say, "I have 15 minutes — show me what you want to show me." So people prefer Zoom calls.

They're faster and shorter, and the customer wants a Zoom call. You want to stay in Israel — everything works well. However, Americans are also somewhat sensitive. I wouldn't call them racist, but Maria is laughing. Yes, they are racist, right? They would never admit it, but they are. So if you have a heavy Russian accent, they are not going to buy from you. And if you speak with an Indian accent and they don't understand what you're saying, they wouldn't buy from you. So you probably want real Americans as salespeople. But you're fortunate — if you cross the street around here, you will meet an American. Every second person is an American. Plenty of Americans in Israel, no problem. And you can manage the work-life, work-family balance.

So in 2003, we were already planning to go back to Israel. And I had a worker called Alex Rinsky, and he said to me one day, "Jonathan, I need to talk to you." He pulls me to the side and says, "Listen, next August, my wife and I decided we're going back to Israel. But I would really love to stay at Zoom and continue selling from Israel." That was before Zoom — we used a video conferencing phone. "I think I can keep my quota from Israel, if you're okay with it." I said, "When in August are you leaving?" He told me, and I said, "I'm leaving two days before you, so welcome to Israel." And he worked in Israel for three or four years as a salesman.

So I asked him, "How do you manage the time difference?" He said, "That's the best thing that ever happened to me." He said, "I wake up in the morning around seven, take the kids to school, come back, eat breakfast with my wife, then just take my time. The kids come back from school, we eat lunch. After lunch, I go to my study, I close the door, and I work from [time] till [time] — that's noon Eastern time. Then I eat dinner with my wife and family. At [time] I go back to the study and keep working till midnight. And then the following day, I wake up and take the kids to school." He says, "I see my kids far more than I ever saw them, and I see my family far more than I used to."

You can create a virtual office in the US if you need to. You'll have an address, you can send mail — everything works. It costs about $30 a month. And if you really need a US presence, my suggestion is pick something around Newark. Why Newark? Which airport? Newark Airport. There are four or five flights a day direct from Israel to Newark. You leave at [time] at night here, you arrive there at [time] in the morning, go to the hotel or apartment, take a shower, have breakfast, go to the office. You leave Sunday night, Monday morning you're in America. Thursday afternoon you go back to the airport, Friday you're home. Nobody even noticed you weren't there. So that's my suggestion.

The other thing is — yes, you can create the company as Israeli. You still need to wire money, pay taxes, deal with regulation. We are kind of semi-experts on that, so if you need help, we'll be delighted to. Okay, we'll deal with that and then I'll start wrapping up.

So, B2B sales cycles can range from one month to years — two to six months is typical. It takes a long time to close a B2B deal, and if you have no leads, you need to start cold calling. And unfortunately, when you close the deal, you don't get the money right away — but your employees want their salary. So the difference in timing is critical. Usually it's Net 60 or Net 90, so even if you close the deal, you won't see the money for another two or three months. And building a lead generation process can easily take six to twelve months. And if you want salespeople, you need to find them, hire them, train them, bring them up to speed. People don't even think about all of that, but it takes forever.

So even if I'm generous to you — from the moment you decide it's time to start selling to the moment you see money in the bank — in my mind, it's two years. I'm quiet on purpose. From the moment you decide you want to start selling to the moment you see money in the bank — it's a long time. Most startups don't start selling before they have a product. By then, they've hired a team, developed the product. They have 20 or 30 people in the company, and their burn rate is at least $400,000–$500,000 a month — that's $5 to $6 million a year. So if you start the sales process well before that, you can save yourself somewhere between $5 and $10 million. That's a lot of money. So just think about it.

The whole presentation today was to tell you: this is a complex process, and the only way to deal with complex processes is to start early. In addition to saving money when you start — and I mentioned this before, but I want to repeat it — if you start selling early, you can identify major issues with your product, the packaging, the true market needs. As I said, the market is an embryonic market. A lot of these things, you want to discover them before you invest all the effort in developing the product. It is much simpler to make a pivot when the company has few employees and just a rough idea of the product. Whenever I hear a company say, "Oh, we just did a pivot," I'm like, "Oh my God, you spent $10 or $15 million and you never checked that you were going in the right direction?" That's scary. So the word "pivot" means they were not here in this lecture — they better come to the lecture and understand it. That won't be hard because I repeated it about five times.

Customers and users are the biggest asset of a company. Own them. Literally own them.

The order of operations — this is critical. Usually it goes: first product, then everything else. I strongly recommend doing them in parallel. You have a product idea — just an idea — and you already start doing branding and lead generation. What are you going to do with the lead generation? You have people who are willing to talk to you. They don't really know what you're doing because you don't really know what you're doing, but they're willing to talk to you — and that's huge. You also solve two problems at once. It's not obvious at first, but you solve two problems at once. One: you found a process that people respond to. Two: you developed the product for the people who respond to you — not the other way around.

Do you understand what I'm saying? Because it's critical. You developed a process to get leads, to get people interested. Now they tell you what they're going to respond to — which is very different from what most people do. Most people think they know everything: they develop the product, and then they need to figure out who is going to respond to them. And many times, the people who respond don't actually want that product. And you pivot. Doing it the other way can save you a lot of money. Then you move to direct sales, get customers, and so forth.

The next point is really critical too. Most entrepreneurs I meet want to conquer the world. Their product is just unbelievable — it does everything: it flies, it dives, it kills, it plays chess. But all the customer wanted was for the chair to stay clean after the meal. That's all they wanted. They don't want the chair to jump. They just want it clean, for God's sake. You don't know that because you feel that the more features you add, the higher the chance people will buy — which is not true. So if you find a simple product at a low cost, you have a customer. Remember: own your customers. See what happens with real customers. You want to have customers.

So look at this table and print it in your memory. Lead generation is the most important growth engine. B2B sales cycles are complex — I think I've convinced you. And keep the prices up — it's much easier to make money that way.

הן מהירות יותר וקצרות יותר, והלקוח רוצה שיחת Zoom. אתם רוצים להישאר בישראל – הכל עובד טוב. עם זאת, אמריקאים הם גם קצת רגישים. לא הייתי קורא להם גזענים, אבל Maria צוחקת. כן, הם גזענים, נכון? הם לעולם לא יודו בזה, אבל הם כן. אז אם יש לכם מבטא רוסי כבד, הם לא יקנו מכם. ואם אתם מדברים במבטא הודי והם לא מבינים מה אתם אומרים, הם לא יקנו מכם. אז כנראה שאתם רוצים אמריקאים אמיתיים כאנשי מכירות. אבל אתם בר מזל – אם תחצו את הרחוב כאן, תפגשו אמריקאי. כל אדם שני הוא אמריקאי. יש הרבה אמריקאים בישראל, אין בעיה. ואתם יכולים לנהל את האיזון עבודה-חיים, עבודה-משפחה.

אז ב-2003, כבר תכננו לחזור לישראל. והיה לי עובד שנקרא Alex Rinsky, והוא אמר לי יום אחד, "Jonathan, אני צריך לדבר איתך." הוא מושך אותי הצידה ואומר, "תקשיב, באוגוסט הבא, אשתי ואני החלטנו לחזור לישראל. אבל אני באמת רוצה להישאר ב-Zoom ולהמשיך למכור מישראל." זה לפני Zoom – השתמשנו בטלפון וידאו קונפרנס. "אני חושב שאני יכול לשמור על ה-quota שלי מישראל, אם אתה מסכים לזה." אמרתי, "מתי באוגוסט אתה עוזב?" הוא סיפר לי, ואמרתי, "אני עוזב יומיים לפניך, אז ברוך הבא לישראל." והוא עבד בישראל שלוש או ארבע שנים כאיש מכירות.

אז שאלתי אותו, "איך אתה מנהל את הפרש השעות?" הוא אמר, "זה הדבר הכי טוב שאי פעם קרה לי." הוא אמר, "אני מתעורר בבוקר בשבע, מוביל את הילדים לבית הספר, חוזר, אוכל ארוחת בוקר עם אשתי, ואז פשוט לוקח את הזמן שלי. הילדים חוזרים מבית הספר, אנחנו אוכלים ארוחת צהריים. אחרי הצהריים, אני הולך ללימוד שלי, סוגר את הדלת, ועובד מ-[שעה] עד [שעה] – זה צהריים שעון מזרח. ואז אני אוכל ארוחת ערב עם אשתי ומשפחה. ב-[שעה] אני חוזר ללימוד וממשיך לעבוד עד חצות. ואז ביום הבא, אני מתעורר ומוביל את הילדים לבית הספר." הוא אומר, "אני רואה את הילדים שלי הרבה יותר ממה שאי פעם ראיתי אותם, ואני רואה את משפחתי הרבה יותר ממה שהייתי רגיל."

אתם יכולים ליצור virtual office בארה"ב אם אתם צריכים. יהיה לכם כתובת, אתם יכולים לשלוח דואר – הכל עובד. עולה בערך $30 בחודש. ואם אתם ממש צריכים נוכחות בארה"ב, ההצעה שלי היא לבחור משהו סביב Newark. למה Newark? איזה שדה תעופה? שדה תעופה Newark. יש ארבע חמש טיסות ביום ישיר מישראל ל-Newark. אתם עוזבים ב-[שעה] בלילה כאן, מגיעים שם ב-[שעה] בבוקר, הולכים למלון או דירה, מתקלחים, אוכלים ארוחת בוקר, הולכים למשרד. עוזבים ביום ראשון בלילה, ביום שני בבוקר אתם באמריקה. ביום חמישי אחר הצהריים הולכים חזרה לשדה התעופה, ביום שישי אתם בבית. אף אחד אפילו לא הבחין שלא הייתם שם. אז זו ההצעה שלי.

הדבר הנוסף הוא – כן, אתם יכולים ליצור את החברה כישראלית. עדיין צריך להעביר כסף, לשלם מסים, להתמודד עם רגולציה. אנחנו סוג של מומחים למחצה בזה, אז אם צריכים עזרה, נשמח. אוקיי, נתמודד עם זה ואז אתחיל לסיים.

אז, B2B sales cycles יכולים לנוע בין חודש אחד לשנים – שניים עד שישה חודשים זה טיפוסי. לוקח הרבה זמן לסגור עסקת B2B, ואם אין לכם leads, צריך להתחיל ב-cold calling. ולצערנו, כשסוגרים את העסקה, לא מקבלים את הכסף מיד – אבל העובדים שלכם רוצים את המשכורת. אז הפרש בעיתוי הוא קריטי. בדרך כלל זה Net 60 או Net 90, אז גם אם סגרתם את העסקה, לא תראו את הכסף למשך עוד חודשיים או שלושה. ובניית תהליך lead generation יכולה לקחת בקלות שישה עד שנים עשר חודשים. ואם אתם רוצים אנשי מכירות, צריך למצוא אותם, לגייס אותם, לאמן אותם, להכשיר אותם. אנשים אפילו לא חושבים על כל זה, אבל זה לוקח לנצח.

אז גם אם אני נדיב אתכם – מהרגע שאתם מחליטים שהגיע הזמן להתחיל למכור ועד הרגע שאתם רואים כסף בבנק – לדעתי, זה שנתיים. אני שותק בכוונה. מהרגע שאתם מחליטים שאתם רוצים להתחיל למכור עד הרגע שאתם רואים כסף בבנק – זה הרבה זמן. רוב הסטארטאפים לא מתחילים למכור לפני שיש להם מוצר. עד אז, גייסו צוות, פיתחו את המוצר. יש להם 20 או 30 אנשים בחברה, ו-burn rate שלהם הוא לפחות $400,000–$500,000 בחודש – זה $5 עד $6 מיליון בשנה. אז אם מתחילים את תהליך המכירות הרבה לפני כן, אתם יכולים לחסוך לעצמכם בין $5 ל-$10 מיליון. זה הרבה כסף. אז פשוט תחשבו על זה.

כל ההצגה היום הייתה לומר לכם: זהו תהליך מורכב, והדרך היחידה להתמודד עם תהליכים מורכבים היא להתחיל מוקדם. בנוסף לחיסכון בכסף כשמתחילים – והזכרתי את זה לפני, אבל אני רוצה לחזור על זה – אם מתחילים למכור מוקדם, אתם יכולים לזהות בעיות גדולות עם המוצר, ה-packaging, הצרכים האמיתיים של השוק. כפי שאמרתי, השוק הוא embryonic. הרבה מהדברים האלה, אתם רוצים לגלות אותם לפני שאתם משקיעים את כל המאמץ בפיתוח המוצר. הרבה יותר פשוט לעשות pivot כשהחברה קטנה ויש רק רעיון גולמי של המוצר. בכל פעם שאני שומע חברה אומרת, "אה, רק עשינו pivot," אני אומר לעצמי, "הו אלוהים, הוצאתם $10 או $15 מיליון ומעולם לא בדקתם שאתם הולכים בכיוון הנכון?" זה מפחיד. אז המילה "pivot" אומרת שהם לא היו כאן בהרצאה הזאת – כדאי שיבואו להרצאה ויבינו את זה. זה לא יהיה קשה כי חזרתי על זה בערך חמש פעמים.

לקוחות ומשתמשים הם הנכס הגדול ביותר של חברה. היו הבעלים שלהם. ממש היו הבעלים שלהם.

סדר הפעולות – זה קריטי. בדרך כלל הוא הולך: קודם מוצר, ואז הכל שאר. אני ממליץ בחום לעשות אותם במקביל. יש לכם רעיון למוצר – רק רעיון – ואתם כבר מתחילים לעשות branding ו-lead generation. מה אתם הולכים לעשות עם ה-lead generation? יש לכם אנשים שמוכנים לדבר אתכם. הם לא ממש יודעים מה אתם עושים כי אתם לא ממש יודעים מה אתם עושים, אבל הם מוכנים לדבר אתכם – וזה עצום. אתם גם פותרים שתי בעיות בבת אחת. זה לא מובן מאליו בהתחלה, אבל אתם פותרים שתי בעיות בבת אחת. אחת: מצאתם תהליך שאנשים מגיבים אליו. שתיים: פיתחתם את המוצר עבור האנשים שמגיבים לכם – לא להפך.

האם אתם מבינים את מה שאני אומר? כי זה קריטי. פיתחתם תהליך לקבל leads, לגרום לאנשים להתעניין. עכשיו הם אומרים לכם למה הם הולכים להגיב – וזה שונה מאוד ממה שרוב האנשים עושים. רוב האנשים חושבים שהם יודעים הכל: הם מפתחים את המוצר, ואחר כך צריכים להבין מי הולך להגיב. והרבה פעמים, האנשים שמגיבים לא רוצים את המוצר הזה. ואתם עושים pivot. עשיית זה בדרך ההפוכה יכולה לחסוך לכם הרבה כסף. אחר כך עוברים למכירות ישירות, מקבלים לקוחות, וכן הלאה.

הנקודה הבאה היא גם קריטית מאוד. רוב היזמים שאני פוגש רוצים לכבוש את העולם. המוצר שלהם הוא פשוט לא יאמן – הוא עושה הכל: הוא עף, הוא צולל, הוא הורג, הוא משחק שחמט. אבל כל מה שהלקוח רצה הוא שהכיסא יישאר נקי אחרי הארוחה. זה הכל שהם רצו. הם לא רוצים שהכיסא יקפץ. הם פשוט רוצים שיהיה נקי, לאלוהים. אתם לא יודעים את זה כי אתם מרגישים שככל שמוסיפים יותר תכונות, גדל הסיכוי שאנשים יקנו – וזה לא נכון. אז אם מוצאים מוצר פשוט במחיר נמוך, יש לכם לקוח. זכרו: היו הבעלים של הלקוחות שלכם. ראו מה קורה עם לקוחות אמיתיים. אתם רוצים לקוחות.

אז הסתכלו על הטבלה הזאת והדפיסו אותה בזיכרון. Lead generation הוא מנוע הצמיחה החשוב ביותר. B2B sales cycles הם מורכבים – אני חושב ששכנעתי אתכם. ושמרו על המחירים גבוהים – הרבה יותר קל לעשות כסף ככה.

Lecture nine of the SmartUp Foundations Course, delivered by Yonatan Stern, offers a comprehensive and practical framework for understanding sales in the context of early-stage startups. Stern structures the session around two broad categories: direct sales, encompassing e-commerce and human salespeople, and indirect sales through channels such as retail, resellers, distributors, and partners. Drawing on his experience with companies like CardScan and ZoomInfo, he uses real-world examples throughout to ground each concept.

A central theme of the lecture is the critical importance of demand generation. Stern is unequivocal: no one will buy a product unless demand is actively created, and any entrepreneur who expects others to generate demand on their behalf is mistaken. Closely linked to this is pricing strategy. Stern explains the concept of price elasticity, noting that consumer and business buyers respond to pricing in fundamentally different ways, and that packaging, pricing, and sales approach are tightly interdependent.

The lecture devotes significant attention to the complexity of B2B sales, which Stern describes as two-dimensional. The first dimension is identifying the right target companies — those for whom the product creates genuine value. The second is navigating the people within those organisations who hold decision-making power. He illustrates how ZoomInfo refined prospect selection not through traditional indicators like industry or geography, but through granular signals such as the number of salespeople in a company or the seniority of the person making contact. He also discusses intent-to-buy data and its potential — and limitations — for improving lead quality.

One of Stern's most emphatic points concerns timing. B2B sales cycles typically run two to six months, lead generation pipelines take six to twelve months to mature, and from the decision to start selling to money appearing in the bank can realistically take two years. Startups that delay commercial activity until the product is fully built face enormous unnecessary burn. Stern strongly advocates starting sales — even with just a rough product idea — in parallel with development. This approach not only saves significant capital but also ensures the product is shaped by actual market feedback rather than internal assumptions.

The lecture closes with a call to treat customers as a company's most valuable asset. Entrepreneurs should resist overloading products with features, focus on solving a simple problem well, and begin lead generation early. Owning the customer relationship from the outset, Stern argues, is the most reliable foundation for long-term growth.
